title: Let justice roll (Amos 5:21–24)
hookLine: God hates empty festivals; let justice roll down like waters

lines: A FESTIVAL AT THE KING'S SHRINE.
cards: Bethel was the king's own shrine in the northern kingdom of Israel, and its festivals were full: offerings, songs, the whole calendar kept.
Then a man from the south, from the village of Tekoa, stood up there and spoke for God, and what he said would empty a room today: I can't stand this. Turn the music off. His name was Amos.
By his own account he wasn't a prophet or a prophet's son, just a herdsman who gathered sycamore figs. And his line has ended up on protest signs.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies." Then: "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs." Noise.

teach.h: OUTSIDE: THE POOR SOLD FOR SHOES.
teach.b: In the chapters around this one, Amos lists what's happening outside the shrine: the poor sold for a pair of shoes, bribes taken at the city gate, the rich lying on beds of ivory.
The festivals went on as if none of it mattered. Then the line: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."
The Hebrew word behind judgment is mishpat, which can also be read as justice: things set right, especially for people who can't defend themselves. Some readers hear a picture underneath.

teach.h: A STREAM THAT NEVER DRIES UP.
teach.b: That land has streams that roar in winter and are dry gullies by summer, and the Hebrew behind mighty can mean ever-flowing, a stream that doesn't fail.

Not a flash flood of good intentions after a sermon: justice that doesn't dry up in August. Christians read this more than one way. Some hear that worship and justice belong together, not that worship is wrong.
Others take it as a warning that God can't be pleased by ceremony that ignores the poor. Either way, the words travel.
In 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. drew on this verse in his well-known speech at the Lincoln Memorial, and Amos's river ran through the civil rights movement.

teach.h: LET JUDGMENT RUN DOWN AS WATERS.
teach.b: A herdsman's sentence at a royal shrine, carried to the steps of a memorial.

how: Christians and churches tie worship to service through food banks, advocacy and giving, and Amos 5:24 has been quoted in Christian movements for civil rights and economic justice.

punishment handed out to those who break the law
things set right, especially for the defenseless

s: Amos was a trained prophet from a prophets' guild
he says he was a herdsman and a tender of fig trees, called away from the flock.
the King James Bible says "let judgment run down as waters"
the Hebrew mishpat can also be read as justice.
Amos says all worship is wrong
he rejects festivals that ignore the poor. some readers hear worship and justice belonging together; others hear a warning.

games.q: you're Amos, a farmer at a packed festival. the music is beautiful, and outside the poor are sold for a pair of shoes. what do you do?
o: join the singing and say nothing.
say, for God, take away the noise of your songs.
go home to your fig trees.
games.why: he speaks for God: "take thou away from me the noise of thy songs." then he asks for justice that flows like a river that never dries up.

practice: Let one unfair thing come to mind, one you can actually see: a coworker always talked over, a neighbor without a ride.

Don't solve it in your head; ask what one small, real step could keep flowing after today, a call, a donation, a word spoken up. If you pray, bring that person or cause to God; if not, simply hold the step in mind.

wordCard.voice: Justice. Mishpat in Hebrew: things set right, especially for people who can't defend themselves, flowing like a stream that never runs dry.

orig.note: Hebrew: justice, judgment, a case set right. the King James usually says judgment.

carryVoice: Your line: justice like a river. Not a flash flood, but a stream that doesn't fail. Day four hundred eighty-four, done.
